PIERCING THE CORPORATE VEIL / ALTER EGO LIABILITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Innovations, Inc.

ALTER EGO / PIERCING THE CORPORATE VEIL INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme Innovations, Inc., a California corporation formed under the law of California. It describes California's common-law "alter ego" doctrine — the equitable doctrine under which a court, in a lawsuit against a corporation or limited liability company, may disregard the separate legal existence of that entity ("pierce the corporate veil") and hold a shareholder, member, or other owner personally liable for the entity's debts, obligations, or other liabilities. Alter ego is not a separate statute or a fixed checklist; it is a judge-made doctrine developed and applied case by case by California courts, and the same doctrine and the same case law govern whether an individual owner, or a parent corporation, can be held liable as the alter ego of a corporation or an LLC it owns or controls. This information sheet does not itself pierce or preserve Acme Innovations, Inc.'s liability shield, does not determine whether Acme Innovations, Inc.'s specific facts would or would not support alter ego liability, and does not evaluate any specific owner's specific liability exposure. Whether the doctrine applies to any particular entity and any particular owner in any particular dispute is a fact-intensive determination made by a court considering the totality of the circumstances presented in that case.

THE TWO-PART TEST FOR ALTER EGO LIABILITY
California courts have long applied a two-part test to decide whether to disregard the corporate (or LLC) entity and hold an owner personally liable under the alter ego doctrine: first, that there be such a unity of interest and ownership between the entity and its equitable owner that the separate personalities of the entity and the owner no longer exist in reality; and second, that treating the entity's acts as its own alone — that is, honoring the separate entity — would bring about an inequitable result. Both parts of the test must be satisfied; unity of interest and ownership alone, without an inequitable result, is not enough to pierce the veil, and California's own courts have said there is no fixed, mechanical test ("litmus test") for when the veil will be pierced — the outcome depends on the circumstances of each particular case. The same two-part test applies, with only a difference in wording, when the owner sought to be held liable is another corporation (for example, a parent corporation held liable for a subsidiary's conduct) rather than an individual shareholder.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It has been stated that the two requirements for application of this doctrine are (1) that there be such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist and (2) that, if the acts are treated as those of the corporation alone, an inequitable result will follow."
  — Automotriz del Golfo de California, S.A. de C.V. v. Resnick, 47 Cal.2d 792, 796 (Cal. 1957) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1392342/automotriz-del-golfo-de-california-v-resnick/)
  "There is no litmus test to determine when the corporate veil will be pierced; rather the result will depend on the circumstances of each particular case. There are, nevertheless, two general requirements: “(1) that there be such unity of interest and ownership that the separate personalities of the corporation and the individual no longer exist and (2) that, if the acts are treated as those of the corporation alone, an inequitable result will follow.” (Automotriz etc. de California v. Resnick (1957) 47 Cal.2d 792, 796 [306 P.2d 1, 63 A.L.R.2d 1042].) And “only a difference in wording is used in stating the same concept where the entity sought to be held liable is another corporation instead of an individual.” (McLoughlin v. L. Bloom Sons Co., Inc. (1962) 206 Cal.App.2d 848, 851 [24 Cal.Rptr. 311].)"
  — Mesler v. Bragg Management Co., 39 Cal.3d 290, 300-301 (Cal. 1985) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1153753/mesler-v-bragg-management-co/)
  Known gap: The two-part test is stated in these terms in Automotriz del Golfo de California, S.A. de C.V. v. Resnick (1957) 47 Cal.2d 792, 796, and is restated verbatim, quoting Automotriz directly, in Mesler v. Bragg Management Co. (1985) 39 Cal.3d 290, 300 ("There is no litmus test to determine when the corporate veil will be pierced; rather the result will depend on the circumstances of each particular case. There are, nevertheless, two general requirements..."). Because Mesler is quoting the identical Automotriz passage rather than independently restating it, these two cases are not independent sources for the wording of the test itself — they are treated here as one source (Automotriz) plus one later California Supreme Court decision confirming that the same wording remains the operative test and extending it, in identical substance, to entity-versus-entity alter ego claims. Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538 independently paraphrases (not quotes) the same two-part test in its own words while citing back to Automotriz, which corroborates that the test has not changed but is likewise not an independently worded source. This is case law, not a statute; no California statute states this general common-law test for corporations. This document does not evaluate whether either part of the test would be met for any specific entity or any specific owner.

FACTORS COURTS CONSIDER — NO FIXED CHECKLIST
California courts have identified a range of factors relevant to whether an entity's separate existence should be disregarded, including: commingling of funds and other assets of the entity and its owner; one party holding out that it is liable for the other's debts; identical equitable ownership between the entity and the person or entity claimed to control it; use of the same offices and employees; treating one as a mere shell or conduit for the affairs of the other; inadequate capitalization; disregard of corporate or entity formalities; failure to segregate records; and identical directors and officers. No single factor is decisive, and no fixed number of factors is required — California courts weigh the totality of the circumstances of each case to decide whether disregarding the entity is warranted. Because alter ego is treated as an extreme remedy, applied sparingly, satisfying some of these factors does not by itself establish alter ego liability; a court must also find that treating the entity's acts as its own alone would produce an inequitable result, and mere difficulty collecting a debt or enforcing a judgment against an entity does not, by itself, meet that standard.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Among the factors to be considered in applying the doctrine are commingling of funds and other assets of the two entities, the holding out by one entity that it is liable for the debts of the other, identical equitable ownership in the two entities, use of the same offices and employees, and use of one as a mere shell or conduit for the affairs of the other. (Roman Catholic Archbishop v. Superior Court, supra, 15 Cal.App.3d at pp. 406, 411; Associated Vendors, Inc. v. Oakland Meat Co., supra, 210 Cal.App.2d at pp. 838-839.) Other factors which have been described in the case law include inadequate capitalization, disregard of corporate formalities, lack of segregation of corporate records, and identical directors and officers. (See Tomaselli v. Transamerica Ins. Co. (1994) 25 Cal.App.4th 1269, 1285 [31 Cal.Rptr.2d 433]; Associated Vendors, Inc. v. Oakland Meat Co., supra, 210 Cal.App.2d at pp. 838-839; Alberto v. Diversified Group, Inc., supra, 55 F.3d at p. 205.) No one characteristic governs, but the courts must look at all the circumstances to determine whether the doctrine should be applied. (Talbot v. Fresno-Pacific Corp. (1960) 181 Cal.App.2d 425, 432 [5 Cal.Rptr. 361].) Alter ego is an extreme remedy, sparingly used."
  — Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court, 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538-539 (Cal. Ct. App. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2250866/sonora-diamond-corp-v-superior-court/)
  "Misconduct or injustice was not proved by Sonora Mining’s apparent inability to meet the balance of its endowment obligation to the District. The alter ego doctrine does not guard every unsatisfied creditor of a corporation but instead affords protectioh where some conduct amounting to bad faith makes it inequitable for the corporate owner to hide behind the corporate form. Difficulty in enforcing a judgment or collecting a debt does not satisfy this standard."
  — Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court, 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 539-540 (Cal. Ct. App. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2250866/sonora-diamond-corp-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This clause draws on Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538-540, a published California Court of Appeal decision, which in turn cites and synthesizes factors identified in earlier California cases (principally Roman Catholic Archbishop v. Superior Court (1971) 15 Cal.App.3d 405 and Associated Vendors, Inc. v. Oakland Meat Co. (1962) 210 Cal.App.2d 825, among others cited within Sonora Diamond itself). This document quotes Sonora Diamond's own restatement of those factors rather than independently re-verifying each underlying case Sonora Diamond cites, so this is effectively one appellate source's synthesis of the factor list, not several independently verified sources. Sonora Diamond itself involved a personal-jurisdiction dispute over a parent/subsidiary relationship, not a judgment-collection case, and the court there found the doctrine did not apply on the facts before it because no inequitable result was shown — illustrating that meeting some of these factors does not guarantee a finding of alter ego liability. This document does not assess whether any specific factor is present for any specific entity or owner.

LLCS ARE TREATED THE SAME AS CORPORATIONS
California has codified that the alter ego doctrine applies to limited liability companies to the same extent it applies to corporations: a member of an LLC is subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and is personally liable for the LLC's debts, obligations, or other liabilities under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for the corporation's debts, obligations, or liabilities. The statute also creates one specific, narrow carve-out: the failure to hold member or manager meetings, or the failure to observe formalities for calling or conducting such meetings, is not by itself a factor tending to establish alter ego or personal liability for an LLC's member — but only where the articles of organization or operating agreement does not itself expressly require holding such meetings. Apart from that one carve-out, the statute does not otherwise limit or list the factors relevant to alter ego liability for an LLC member; it incorporates the same common-law doctrine, and the same case law, that governs corporate shareholders.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "All of the following apply to debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a limited liability company, whether arising in contract, tort, or otherwise: (1) They are solely the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of the limited liability company to which the debts, obligations, or other liabilities relate. (2) They do not become the debts, obligations, or other liabilities of a member or manager solely by reason of the member acting as a member or manager acting as a manager for the limited liability company."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, general LLC liability shield (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17703.04.)
  "A member of a limited liability company shall be subject to liability under the common law governing alter ego liability, and shall also be personally liable under a judgment of a court or for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company, whether that liability or obligation arises in contract, tort, or otherwise, under the same or similar circumstances and to the same extent as a shareholder of a corporation may be personally liable for any debt, obligation, or liability of the corporation; except that the failure to hold meetings of members or managers or the failure to observe formalities pertaining to the calling or conduct of meetings shall not be considered a factor tending to establish that a member or the members have alter ego or personal liability for any debt, obligation, or liability of the limited liability company where the articles of organization or operating agreement do not expressly require the holding of meetings of members or managers."
  — Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, alter ego liability and the meeting-formalities carve-out (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CORP&sectionNum=17703.04.)
  Known gap: This is a single California statute (Cal. Corp. Code § 17703.04(a)-(b)), part of the California Revised Uniform Limited Liability Company Act, used here as direct statutory evidence that California law extends the common-law alter ego doctrine to LLC members on the same terms as corporate shareholders — not a claim about any other state's law, and not a claim about the alter ego doctrine as applied to any specific California LLC or member. This clause's two citations are subdivisions of the same statutory section (17703.04(a) and (b)), not independently sourced provisions; they are reproduced together because subdivision (a) establishes the baseline liability shield that subdivision (b) then subjects to the common-law alter ego exception. This corpus's Single-Member LLC Operating Agreement document already cites subdivision (a) and (b) together for the liability-shield side of this same statute; this clause cites the identical statutory text for the alter ego side specifically. This document does not determine whether any specific LLC has held member or manager meetings, or whether its governing documents require them.

AN EQUITABLE DOCTRINE, NOT A DISSOLUTION OF THE ENTITY
The alter ego doctrine is an equitable doctrine for imposing liability, not a mechanism that dissolves or merges the entity itself. When a court disregards an entity's separate existence for alter ego purposes, it does not hold that the entity and its owner were "really" only ever one and the same for all purposes; rather, the entity continues to exist, and the court instead permits the owner to be held liable, alongside the entity, for a particular debt or judgment because equity requires that result under the circumstances of that case. The doctrine arises when a party claims that another party is using the entity form unjustly and to that party's detriment, and the corporate form will be disregarded only in narrowly defined circumstances, and only when the ends of justice require it — not automatically whenever an entity's owner exercises control over it, and not merely because a creditor has difficulty collecting from the entity itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is not that a corporation will be held liable for the acts of another corporation because there is really only one corporation. Rather, it is that under certain circumstances a hole will be drilled in the wall of limited liability erected by the corporate form; for all purposes other than that for which the hole was drilled, the wall still stands. When it is claimed that a parent corporation should be liable because it is the alter ego of its subsidiary, equity commands that the corporate wall be breached. Yet the wall remains: the parent is liable through the acts of the subsidiary, but as a separate entity."
  — Mesler v. Bragg Management Co., 39 Cal.3d 290, 300-301 (Cal. 1985) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1153753/mesler-v-bragg-management-co/)
  "A corporate identity may be disregarded—the “corporate veil” pierced—where an abuse of the corporate privilege justifies holding the equitable ownership of a corporation liable for the actions of the corporation. (Roman Catholic Archbishop v. Superior Court (1971) 15 Cal.App.3d 405, 411 [93 Cal.Rptr. 338].) Under the alter ego doctrine, then, when the corporate form is used to perpetrate a fraud, circumvent a statute, or accomplish some other wrongful or inequitable purpose, the courts will ignore the corporate entity and deem the corporation’s acts to be those of the persons or organizations actually controlling the corporation, in most instances the equitable owners."
  — Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court, 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538 (Cal. Ct. App. 2000) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2250866/sonora-diamond-corp-v-superior-court/)
  Known gap: This clause draws on the California Supreme Court's discussion in Mesler v. Bragg Management Co. (1985) 39 Cal.3d 290, 300-301, describing the alter ego doctrine's equitable character and its effect (a parent corporation held liable as alter ego of a subsidiary remains, and is sued as, a separate entity — "the wall remains" even though "a hole will be drilled" in it for that purpose), and on Sonora Diamond Corp. v. Superior Court (2000) 83 Cal.App.4th 523, 538, which independently states that the corporate form is disregarded only "where an abuse of the corporate privilege justifies" it. These are two different, independently worded California appellate sources describing the same general equitable character of the doctrine, though both ultimately trace the same body of common law. Neither case holds, in so many words, that "alter ego" is not itself an independent cause of action separate from the underlying claim against the entity; this document does not make that specific characterization because it was not independently verified against primary case text within the scope of this research, and it is omitted rather than asserted on the strength of secondary sources alone.

Executed on September 2, 2026 at Sacramento, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

[This information sheet describes California's common-law alter ego doctrine, the two-part test and factors California courts have applied under it, and the statute extending the doctrine to limited liability company members on the same terms as corporate shareholders. It is educational only. It does not determine whether Acme Innovations, Inc.'s separate legal existence would or would not be disregarded in any specific dispute, does not evaluate any specific owner's personal liability exposure, and does not constitute legal advice. Whether alter ego liability applies to any specific entity, owner, or set of facts is a determination made by a court, not by this document.]
